title: Physical AI Pushes The Limits Of Hardware
gist: Physical AI (robots, drones, vehicles), projected by PwC's Strategy& at roughly EUR 430 billion by 2030, is constrained less by compute than by a memory wall, power/thermal limits and safety validation. Industry voices from Synopsys, Arteris, Micron, Siemens EDA, Analog Devices, Imagination and Rambus point to workload-specific ASICs and chiplets, low-bit formats, faster LPDDR6/UFS interfaces, and possibly a new physical-AI-specific memory category.

themes.theme: Physical AI market size and scope

insights.claim: PwC's Strategy& projects the global physical AI market could reach approximately EUR 430 billion by 2030, spanning transportation, manufacturing, medicine and energy.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Provides a third-party TAM anchor for robotics, autonomy and edge-silicon investment cases.

insights.claim: Synopsys' Licinio Sousa says physical AI is expanding beyond automotive to robotics and drones, driven by needs for autonomy, privacy, personalization, faster response and less cloud reliance.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Broadens the end-market for automotive-grade edge silicon and interface IP.

themes.theme: Return to workload-specific ASICs and chiplets

insights.claim: Arteris' Michal Siwinski argues physical AI is driving a return to ASICs in the traditional sense, with compute highly tailored and optimized for specific workloads rather than generic, a shift he says has already started.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Benefits custom-silicon enablers such as NoC IP, EDA and design-services firms over general-purpose processors.
insights.quote: We’re basically going back to ASICs in the traditional sense of what ASICs were supposed to be

insights.claim: Sousa says the spread of physical AI use cases and demand for vision-language-action (VLA) models is pushing a transition from monolithic architectures to chiplets that scale compute, AI, memory and I/O via UCIe.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Supports demand for UCIe die-to-die IP and advanced packaging in edge/robotics silicon.

insights.claim: The article notes chiplets raise cost and complexity through custom packaging, thermal management and die-to-die communication, so monolithic SoCs may remain preferable for small, power-, size- and cost-constrained systems.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Tempers the chiplet thesis: high-volume low-cost robotics may stay monolithic.

insights.claim: Micron's Vasanthan Karunanithy says robotics inherits perception, path planning and motion control from ADAS and language reasoning from intelligent cabins, but must run both together in unstructured 3D environments on a far more limited power source than a vehicle battery.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Automotive silicon roadmaps are the on-ramp to robotics, but power budgets demand more efficient parts.
insights.quote: Robotics is not a new AI stack
insights.locator: “Robotics is not a new AI stack,”

insights.claim: Analog Devices' Yasmine King describes a push-pull in intelligence placement: centralized compute simplifies over-the-air updates and patching, while distributed intelligence near sensors cuts latency for time-critical reactions like a pedestrian stepping in front of a car.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Architecture choice determines whether value accrues to central SoC vendors or distributed sensor/edge-chip suppliers.

insights.claim: Memory capacity, bandwidth, latency and energy are the key physical AI chokepoints, alongside potential supply constraints for some memory technologies, and Sousa says DRAM needs ultra-fast interfaces such as LPDDR6 to stop bottlenecking processing.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Supports LPDDR6 adoption and memory content growth per robot/vehicle, with supply tightness as a pricing tailwind.
insights.quote: DRAM needs an ultra-fast interface, such as LPDDR6, to no longer be a bottleneck to processing.

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's Sathish Balasubramanian argues for right-sized memory using a 'Prius needs a 10-gallon tank, not 100' analogy: keep critical data in DRAM but lean on cache, built-in SRAM and flash to avoid huge DRAM footprints.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: A counterpoint suggesting physical AI DRAM content per device may be smaller than bulls assume.
insights.quote: You don’t need a 100-gallon tank in your Prius. You need a 10-gallon tank.

insights.claim: Imagination's Rob Fisher says most robotics requirements come directly from automotive, many automotive players now market chips as automotive-and-robotics platforms, and 4-, 6- and 8-bit support will be used to shrink memory footprint and bandwidth rather than enlarge models.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Automotive chip vendors gain a second robotics revenue stream with existing platforms.
insights.quote: A lot of automotive players will now present their chips as automotive and robotics platforms
insights.locator: “It’s very closely coupled to our automotive

insights.claim: Sousa says DRAM is constrained in capacity, power and availability, so faster storage bandwidth (UFS, PCIe) that shortens model load times lets the same DRAM budget support larger models in battery-powered, often passively cooled systems.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Raises the value of fast NAND/UFS storage and low-power interface IP in robotics bills of materials.
insights.quote: DRAM is constrained in capacity, power, and availability
insights.locator: Flash storage also plays a critical role

insights.claim: Rambus' Steven Woo says physical AI could grow large enough to warrant its own memory type or variant, as happened when HBM emerged and when phones moved from binned low-power DDR parts to purpose-built LPDDR.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: A potential new memory product category would create opportunities for memory makers and interface IP licensors like Rambus.
insights.quote: Physical AI has the potential to become a big enough market on its own, so that if the requirements vary enough, there could be another kind of memory.

insights.claim: Balasubramanian calls the pre-production validation loop the most important task for physical AI, requiring local compute, memory and intelligence near sensors to handle scenarios like power cuts, earthquakes or severed fiber connections.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Validation and verification tooling becomes a gating spend item for physical AI deployment.
insights.quote: The validation loop that we need to bring physical AI into before we get into any production is paramount

insights.claim: ATDev co-founder Owen Kent says assistive robotics such as wheelchairs require hardware to pass quality management and third-party electromagnetic compatibility testing regardless of whether it is custom.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Certification burden lengthens time-to-market for medical and assistive robotics startups.
insights.locator: “When we’re designing something for a wheelchair

insights.claim: The MIPI Camera Security Framework, combining Camera Service Extensions 2.0 with security specs, provides integrity protection, authentication and optional encryption of CSI-2 camera data from image sensor to SoC, letting designers scale security to the application.
insights.speaker: Brendan Heffernan
insights.so_what: Standards-based camera security adds IP and silicon content in autonomous sensor chains.
